title: String handling, conversions, and files for your project

resources.label: Learn C#
resources.note: Our C# practice site. Type each example in, run it, and change it. C# is one of the languages AQA accepts in the exam.

steps.title: Strings are sequences of characters
steps.body:
A **string** is text: a sequence of characters, each with an **index** starting at 0, just like an array. AQA gives you four built-in operations:

- `LEN(s)`: the number of characters.
- `SUBSTRING(start, end, s)`: the characters from index `start` to index `end`, **both included**.
- `POSITION(s, c)`: the index of the first `c` in `s`. AQA does not say what it gives back when the character is not there, so in an exam say in words what you are checking, or use the value your language returns (−1 in Python and C#, 0 in VB.NET).
- `+`: **concatenation**, joining two strings.

```
word ← 'computer'
OUTPUT LEN(word)
OUTPUT SUBSTRING(0, 2, word)
OUTPUT POSITION(word, 'p')
```

Output: `8`, `com`, `3`.

visuals.alt: A table with the indexes 0 to 7 in the top row and the letters of computer beneath them

steps.text: Number the characters first: c 0, o 1, m 2, p 3, u 4, t 5, e 6, r 7
`SUBSTRING(3, 5, word)` takes indexes 3, 4 **and** 5, because both ends are included
steps.note: end − start + 1 characters, so three, not two

steps.text: Those characters are p, u, t, so the result is `put`
steps.note: read them straight off the index list

steps.text: `POSITION(word, 't')` is the index of the first t, which is 5
`SUBSTRING(0, 0, word)` is the single character `c`
steps.note: the same index twice picks one character

check.solution: Indexes 4 and 5 are u and t.

steps.title: Joining and measuring
steps.body:
`+` joins strings. It does not add a space, so put one in yourself.

```
first ← 'Ada'
last ← 'Lovelace'
full ← first + ' ' + last
OUTPUT full
OUTPUT LEN(full)
```

Output: `Ada Lovelace` then `12`. The space counts as a character.

steps.text: age is a number, so convert it first: INT_TO_STRING(age)
name + ' (' + INT_TO_STRING(age) + ')'
Result: Sam (15), which is 8 characters long

steps.title: Converting between types
steps.body:
Numbers and text look alike but behave differently. `12 + 3` is 15; `'12' + '3'` is `'123'`. Four conversions:

- `STRING_TO_INT('12')` gives the whole number 12, and `STRING_TO_REAL('12.5')` gives the decimal 12.5.
- `INT_TO_STRING(12)` gives the text `'12'`, and `REAL_TO_STRING(12.5)` gives the text `'12.5'`.
- `CHAR_TO_CODE('A')` gives the character code, 65.
- `CODE_TO_CHAR(66)` gives `'B'`.

```
OUTPUT CHAR_TO_CODE('A')
OUTPUT CODE_TO_CHAR(66)
OUTPUT STRING_TO_INT('12') + 3
OUTPUT INT_TO_STRING(12) + '3'
```

Output: `65`, `B`, `15`, `123`. Everything typed with `USERINPUT` and everything read from a file is a **string**, so convert before doing maths.

visuals.problem: A student writes total ← USERINPUT + 5 and gets an error

steps.text: USERINPUT returns a string, and a string cannot be added to 5
Convert first: total ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT) + 5
Now the input 10 gives 15, not '105' or a crash

options: 45 as a number

steps.title: Looping through a string
steps.body:
Because a string has indexes, you can loop over it like an array. `SUBSTRING(i, i, text)` picks out one character.

AQA pseudo-code also has a loop that walks a string directly, without indexes:

```
count ← 0
FOR char IN text
   IF char = 'a' THEN
      count ← count + 1
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
```

The same loop reverses a string in a few lines, and this is the version AQA's own pseudo-code guide shows:

```
reversed ← ''
FOR char IN message
   reversed ← char + reversed
ENDFOR
```

Use whichever you find clearer, but be ready to read `FOR char IN` in an exam question.

visuals.problem: Count the letter a in banana

steps.text:
```
text ← 'banana'
count ← 0
FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(text) - 1
   IF SUBSTRING(i, i, text) = 'a' THEN
      count ← count + 1
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT count
```
Six characters, indexes 0 to 5
a is at indexes 1, 3 and 5: count ends at 3

visuals.alt: Trace of counting a in banana

check.prompt: With `text ← 'mississippi'` and the same program counting `'s'`, what is output?
check.solution: m-i-s-s-i-s-s-i-p-p-i has four s, so the output is **4**.

steps.title: Files: saving data between runs
steps.body:
Variables vanish when a program ends. To keep data, write it to a **file**. AQA does not examine file handling: it is not in the 8525 specification and there is no file syntax in AQA pseudo-code. Your Year 10 programming project uses files, though, so here is the pattern most textbooks use:

1. **Open** the file for writing or reading.
2. **Write** lines, or **read** lines until `endOfFile()`.
3. **Close** the file, so the data is saved and the file is released.

```
myFile ← openWrite('scores.txt')
myFile.writeLine('Sam,42')
myFile.writeLine('Ali,37')
myFile.close()

myFile ← openRead('scores.txt')
WHILE NOT myFile.endOfFile()
   line ← myFile.readLine()
   OUTPUT line
ENDWHILE
myFile.close()
```

Output: `Sam,42` then `Ali,37`. Everything read back is a **string**; the 42 has to be converted before it is used as a number.

visuals.problem: Why loop with WHILE NOT endOfFile rather than a FOR loop?

steps.text: The program does not know how many lines the file has
endOfFile() becomes True when there is nothing left to read
So the loop reads exactly the lines that exist, however many there are

check.prompt: What happens to the data written with `writeLine` if the program never calls `close()`?
check.solution: Close flushes the buffer. Missing it is the classic file bug.
options: Some or all of it may not be saved, because writing is buffered until the file is closed
It is saved twice, because the program writes it again when it finishes running
It is saved but cannot be read, because the file stays locked for other programs
Nothing happens: close is optional and the data is written as soon as writeLine runs

steps.title: Your turn: reverse a string
steps.body:
Write code that builds the reverse of `word`. Plan: an empty result string, a loop from the **last** index down to 0, adding one character each time. Then test whether the word is a palindrome by comparing the two.

Try it on our [Learn C#](https://red-dune-0f7372e10.7.azurestaticapps.net/) site with `word[i]` and a `for` loop counting down.

steps.text:
```
word ← 'level'
reversed ← ''
FOR i ← LEN(word) - 1 TO 0 STEP -1
   reversed ← reversed + SUBSTRING(i, i, word)
ENDFOR
OUTPUT reversed = word
```
STEP −1 makes the loop count down: 4, 3, 2, 1, 0
reversed becomes l, le, lev, leve, level
level = level is True

check.prompt: With `word ← 'stop'`, what value does `reversed` hold when the loop ends?

steps.title: Grade 9: files plus strings plus types
steps.body:
The hardest questions chain the ideas: take a line of text (in the exam it comes from USERINPUT; in your project it comes from a file), split it into parts, convert a part to a number, then do something with it. Keep the sequence in your head: **read** (string), **find** the comma with `POSITION`, **cut** with `SUBSTRING`, **convert** with `STRING_TO_INT`, **use**.

When writing code in the exam, open before the loop, close after it, and initialise counters before the loop. Say what a function returns rather than outputting inside it.

visuals.problem: Read 'Sam,42' from a file and get the score as a number

steps.text: p ← POSITION(line, ',') gives 3
name ← SUBSTRING(0, p - 1, line) gives Sam
score ← STRING_TO_INT(SUBSTRING(p + 1, LEN(line) - 1, line)) gives 42 as a number

check.solution: P-r-i-y-a are indexes 0 to 4; the comma is at 5.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Strings are indexed from 0. LEN, SUBSTRING(start, end, s) with both ends included, POSITION, and + for joining.
- Convert between types: STRING_TO_INT, INT_TO_STRING, CHAR_TO_CODE, CODE_TO_CHAR. Input and file data are strings.
- Loop over a string with SUBSTRING(i, i, s) to count, reverse or check characters.
- Files: open, read with WHILE NOT endOfFile or write lines, then close.
- Chain them: read, POSITION, SUBSTRING, STRING_TO_INT, use.

visuals.alt: Reference table of string functions and results

questions.solution: The + joins two strings together: concatenation.

questions.prompt: Which built-in function turns the text `'42'` into the number 42 so it can be used in a calculation?
questions.solution: Input arrives as a string. STRING_TO_INT converts it before you add to it.
options: STRING_TO_INT
INT_TO_STRING
CHAR_TO_CODE
LEN

questions.prompt: Project practice, not examined by AQA: why must a program close a file after writing to it?
questions.solution: Writing is buffered. Closing flushes the data to the file and releases it.
options: So the data is saved properly and the file is released for other programs to use
So the file is deleted from the disk and the space it used is made free again
So the file becomes read-only and no other program can change what was written
Closing makes no difference; it is optional and only tidies up the code

questions.prompt:
What is output by the third line of this program?

```
word ← 'computer'
OUTPUT LEN(word)
OUTPUT SUBSTRING(0, 2, word)
OUTPUT POSITION(word, 'p')
```
questions.solution: In AQA pseudo-code SUBSTRING(start, end, string) takes characters from index start to index end, both included. Indexes 0, 1, 2 of computer are c, o, m: "com".

questions.prompt:
What is output by the last line of this program?

```
first ← 'Ada'
last ← 'Lovelace'
full ← first + ' ' + last
OUTPUT full
OUTPUT LEN(full)
```
questions.solution: Ada plus a space plus Lovelace is 3 + 1 + 8 = 12 characters.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between `STRING_TO_INT('12') + 3` and `INT_TO_STRING(12) + '3'`, giving the result of each.
questions.solution: The point is that + means add for numbers and join for strings.

criteria.text: STRING_TO_INT makes 12 a number, so + adds: result 15
INT_TO_STRING makes 12 a string, so + concatenates: result "123"
The type of the values decides whether + adds or joins

questions.modelAnswer: STRING_TO_INT('12') turns the text into the number 12, so + 3 adds and the result is 15. INT_TO_STRING(12) turns the number into the text '12', so + '3' joins the two strings and the result is '123'. The same symbol does different jobs depending on the data types.

questions.prompt: Project practice, not examined by AQA: a file is opened with `openRead` and read line by line in a loop. Which condition should control the loop?
questions.solution: Keep reading until the end-of-file check says there is nothing left. A fixed count fails if the file changes length.
options: WHILE NOT myFile.endOfFile()
WHILE myFile.readLine()
FOR i ← 0 TO 10
WHILE myFile.close()

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
text ← 'banana'
count ← 0
FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(text) - 1
   IF SUBSTRING(i, i, text) = 'a' THEN
      count ← count + 1
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT count
```
questions.solution: The loop checks every character; banana has three letter a, so the output is **3**.

questions.prompt: Write a function `initials(first, last)` that returns the first letter of each name joined together in capitals, so `initials('ada', 'lovelace')` returns `'AL'`. You may use `SUBSTRING` and assume a function `UPPER(text)` exists.
questions.solution: Take one character from each with SUBSTRING, join them, convert to upper case, return.

markScheme.description: SUBSTRING for first letter of first
SUBSTRING for first letter of last

criteria.text: SUBSTRING(0, 0, first) and SUBSTRING(0, 0, last) to take the first characters
UPPER applied to the result, or to each letter

questions.modelAnswer:
```
SUBROUTINE initials(first, last)
   a ← SUBSTRING(0, 0, first)
   b ← SUBSTRING(0, 0, last)
   RETURN UPPER(a + b)
ENDSUBROUTINE
```

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
word ← 'level'
reversed ← ''
FOR i ← LEN(word) - 1 TO 0 STEP -1
   reversed ← reversed + SUBSTRING(i, i, word)
ENDFOR
OUTPUT reversed = word
```
questions.solution: The loop builds the word backwards: level reversed is level, so the comparison is True. A word that reads the same backwards is a palindrome.

questions.prompt: Project practice, not examined by AQA: a program stores high scores in a text file, one per line as `name,score`. When the program reads the file back, what must it do before comparing scores as numbers?
questions.solution: Files hold characters. The score comes back as the string "42" and must be converted before it can be compared or added.
options: Split each line at the comma and convert the score part with STRING_TO_INT, because everything read from a file is text
Nothing: numbers written to a file stay numbers, so the score can be compared as soon as it is read
Convert the name part with INT_TO_STRING, because names are read from a file as numbers
Read the file twice, once to get the names and once to get the scores, then compare the two lists

questions.prompt: `CHAR_TO_CODE('a')` is 97. What does `CODE_TO_CHAR(CHAR_TO_CODE('a') + 2)` return? Give the character.
questions.solution: 97 + 2 = 99, and the character with code 99 is c: the letters run in order in ASCII.

questions.prompt: Project practice, not examined by AQA. For your programming project: a program must read every line of `names.txt` and count how many lines contain the letter `z` anywhere. Write the program, using a `FOR char IN` loop to look for the letter.
questions.solution: Open, loop until end of file, search the line character by character, count, close, output. Searching with a loop avoids relying on what POSITION returns when the letter is missing.

markScheme.description: Search each character with a flag, count + 1

criteria.text: Open the file for reading and close it at the end
A count variable set to 0 before the loop
WHILE NOT endOfFile loop reading a line each time
A FOR char IN loop, or equivalent, that sets a flag when a z is found, and count + 1 if the flag is set
Output the count after the loop

questions.modelAnswer:
```
myFile ← openRead('names.txt')
count ← 0
WHILE NOT myFile.endOfFile()
   line ← myFile.readLine()
   hasZ ← False
   FOR char IN line
      IF char = 'z' THEN
         hasZ ← True
      ENDIF
   ENDFOR
   IF hasZ THEN
      count ← count + 1
   ENDIF
ENDWHILE
myFile.close()
OUTPUT count
```

questions.prompt: Why does a program reading user input with `USERINPUT` usually need `STRING_TO_INT` before doing arithmetic?
questions.solution: Everything typed at the keyboard arrives as text.
options: USERINPUT always returns a string, even when the user types digits, so it must be converted before it can be used as a number
USERINPUT returns a real number, and STRING_TO_INT rounds it to the nearest whole number before arithmetic
STRING_TO_INT removes the spaces and punctuation from the input so that the arithmetic does not fail
Arithmetic only works on strings, so the number has to be converted into text before it can be added

questions.prompt: A program reads the string '3.5' from the user and needs to multiply it by 2. Which conversion does it need?
questions.solution: The value has a decimal point, so STRING_TO_INT would lose the .5 or fail. STRING_TO_REAL gives the real number 3.5.
options: STRING_TO_REAL, because the value has a decimal part
STRING_TO_INT, because all numbers typed in are integers
REAL_TO_STRING, because the answer will be printed
INT_TO_STRING, because 3.5 rounds to 4 first

examTechnique.body: String questions ask what a line outputs, what a loop counts, or for code that builds or checks a string. Know that SUBSTRING includes both ends in AQA pseudo-code, that indexes start at 0, and that FOR char IN walks a string directly. Convert anything numeric that arrives as text. File handling is not examined by AQA; it is here for your programming project.
examinerErrors: Treating SUBSTRING(0, 2, s) as two characters. In AQA pseudo-code it is three: indexes 0, 1 and 2.
Adding a number to USERINPUT or to a value read from a file without converting it first.
Forgetting the space when joining a first name and a surname.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer indexes strings from 0 without slipping, converts types at the right moment, chains POSITION, SUBSTRING and STRING_TO_INT to pull a number out of a line of text, and writes file code with open, loop, close and a counter set up before the loop.
